How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability).

Provenance, kept so that a TRACE Research Object (TRO) declaration of the run can be written later from a stored result (metacheck #404; the helpers are in R/provenance.R). Only when code was run (execute = TRUE): * run_results$started_at, run_results$ended_at: when each run of a script started and ended (ISO 8601, UTC, milliseconds); NA for a script that was not started. A script run again in a later pass has the times of its last run. A TRO uses them for each trov:TransparentResearchPerformance. * run_results$exit_status: the exit status of the process that ran the script (0 = ended normally); NA when the process did not report one (a time limit, or Docker failing to start the container). * artifacts: one row per file, with stage (deposit: as downloaded from the repository, hashed from the downloaded file; before_run: the run folder just before the first script ran, after metacheck’s own changes, such as rewritten paths and unpacked archives; after_run: only the files the scripts made (status new), changed (changed) or removed (removed), as an unchanged file is the one listed before the run), path (relative to the run folder, as valid UTF-8, a byte of another encoding written as <xx>), size (bytes), sha256, mime_type (by extension, NA when unknown), source (the file’s address in the repository, for deposit). The package libraries metacheck installs in the run folder are left out, as are metacheck’s own files there (a script’s runner, and the statistical output it writes in statistical_output/). Files metacheck itself copied or made between passes (see modifications, output_copied, file_placed) show in after_run too. A TRO uses the rows as trov:ResearchArtifacts and each stage as a trov:ArtifactArrangement. * modifications$sha256_before, modifications$sha256_after: the hash of the changed script as downloaded and as it ran; NA when the script is not at the same path in both (a script made from an R Markdown file). * environment: the system that ran the code (trov:TransparentResearchSystem in a TRO): metacheck_version, started_at, ended_at, host (R version, platform, operating system), sandbox, network_isolated (TRUE only when every Docker run had --network none; the process sandbox does not stop the network), internet, timeout_per_script, total_timeout, python_local (the Python run outside Docker and its version), and docker: runs (for each kind of run, r_run, r_install, python_run, python_install, the image and the docker run arguments, such as --network none, --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, the process limit and the memory and processor limits) and images (for each image, its ID and digests from docker image inspect, its creation time and the R and Python versions its environment declares).

run_results$checked says what the run of each script shows about the code, in five groups, so that a script that does not reproduce is kept apart from one the check could not test: ran (it ran to the end); code_error (it did not reproduce: it stopped with an error of the code or the deposit, could not be read, or needs a file the deposit does not hold); dependency (a package or program was not available: a package that could not be installed or was not loaded, a program outside R and Python, a system library, or R crashing in a package’s compiled code); time (it did not finish within the time limit for one script, or was not started because the time for all scripts had run out); and not_checkable (it could not be checked automatically: it needs a person, the internet, a key or another setting of the authors’ computer, one platform such as Google Colab, Windows or OpenSAFELY, more memory than the run allows, a file that was not downloaded, a screen, or a program that runs it, or it is a file of a package of the code that Python runs only as a module of that package). It is NA for files run inside another script, files that are not an analysis, files not read, and a Docker failure. summary_table counts each group (repro_ran_n, repro_code_error_n, repro_dependency_n, repro_time_n, repro_not_checkable_n), and the report’s first sentence gives them. The traffic light reflects the static readiness signals by default; a script in code_error that stopped with an error makes it red, as a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure, and a script in one of the other three groups keeps it from being green. Calls that need a screen, which the run does not have (dev.print(), dev.copy2pdf(), dev.copy2eps(), savePlot(), windows(), win.graph(), x11(), quartz(), View()), are replaced before the run by calls that need none, which modifications records as screen_call_replaced. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

The item-level analyses were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/ka7d8). The analysis code, the item and label texts, the embeddings, and the results are available at https://osf.io/4s63z.

Introduction

Psychology has a measurement problem: different constructs often share the same name, and the same construct is measured under different names. Thorndike (1904) and Kelley (1927) described these as the jingle and jangle fallacies, one construct name used for measures of different constructs, or different construct names for measures of the same construct, and attributed them to a vague connection between psychological theory and its operationalization (Hanfstingl et al., 2024). Both rest on the assumption that a measure's name indicates what it contains (Elson et al., 2023). The assumption can be checked against two sources of evidence, the items a measure contains and the responses those items elicit, and both fallacies appear at both levels. In the items, one name can cover different content: seven widely used depression scales together cover 52 symptoms, with low average overlap (Fried, 2017), seven self-report scales for obsessive-compulsive symptoms in youth share few of the 54 symptoms they assess (Visontay et al., 2019), and measures of general mental health in early and middle adolescence overlap little in content (Black et al., 2023). Different names can also cover the same content: grit items such as "I finish whatever I begin" and "I am a hard worker" are hard to tell apart from conscientiousness items such as "I carry out my plans" and "I work hard" (Henry et al., 2024). In participants' responses, measures with different names can be nearly redundant: job satisfaction and organizational commitment, conceptually distinct, correlated .91 once corrected for measurement error (Le et al., 2010), and grit correlated .84 with conscientiousness after the same correction (Credé et al., 2017). Measures administered under one name can also reflect more than one construct: measures of adolescent autonomy in the family reflected two distinct dimensions (Van Petegem et al., 2013). When the assumption fails, subscales may be entered as separate predictors in the same models, differences between them may receive a clinical interpretation, and researchers and reviews may group them under headings that assume they are distinct, when they may not be. Current review and meta-analytic methods do not detect these fallacies (Hanfstingl et al., 2024), since studies are selected and grouped by the construct names they report: a jingle pools measures of different constructs under one heading, and a jangle keeps measures of the same construct under separate ones. Wulff and Mata (2025) highlight the resulting taxonomic incommensurability: findings obtained under different construct taxonomies are difficult to compare and integrate.

We argue that the problem weighs particularly on clinical psychology, a discipline concerned with meaning. People communicate their emotions, intentions, and patterns of behavior through language, and clinicians rely on these accounts to understand distress and adaptive functioning. Self-report questionnaires, the most widely used instruments in clinical and developmental research, are themselves made of language. Each item is a condensed description of a psychological state or tendency, and participants' responses indicate how they understood and endorsed that description (Schwarz, 1999). The validity of a measure therefore depends on the meaning of its wording as well as on its statistical properties (Borsboom et al., 2004; Maul, 2017). The construct name is language too: it says what the items are taken to measure, and it is the basis on which findings obtained with different instruments are compared and grouped in reviews and meta-analyses. Construct names and items thus stand at the two ends of the connection between theory and operationalization, and both can be compared as language.

Mentalizing, Epistemic Trust, and Emotion Regulation

The problem might be particularly evident for constructs that theory describes as interdependent, and we take the mentalizing framework as a case study. Mentalizing is the capacity to understand the self and others in terms of intentional mental states, such as feelings, desires, wishes, attitudes, and goals (Bateman & Fonagy, 2016; Luyten et al., 2020). It is linked to epistemic trust (ET), an individual's willingness to consider new knowledge from another person as trustworthy, generalizable, and relevant to the self (Fonagy & Allison, 2014), which is both facilitated by and facilitates mentalizing (Luyten et al., 2020). The experience of having one's own subjectivity understood, of being mentalized, is thought to open epistemic trust and, with it, the possibility of learning from social communication (Fonagy & Allison, 2014).

Mentalizing and emotion regulation are linked in a circular way: stress and arousal shift mentalizing from controlled to automatic and often biased modes (Luyten et al., 2020), and "mentalizing difficulties lead to affect dysregulation, which in turn further disrupts mentalizing" (Fonagy et al., 2017, p. 4). Together, these capacities form a social learning system through which individuals acquire and update knowledge about themselves and the social world in communication with trusted others, and disruptions of this system have been proposed to underlie a general vulnerability to psychopathology, captured by the p-factor, and personality pathology (Fonagy et al., 2017; Luyten et al., 2020).

Both fallacies, at both levels, are visible in this domain. Within the framework itself, mentalizing is described as "an umbrella concept that overlaps with a range of constructs and capacities, such as Theory of Mind (ToM), mindfulness, perspective taking, and empathy" (Luyten et al., 2020, p. 300). In the content of the measures, one construct name covers many instruments: a systematic review of questionnaire, interview, and text-coding measures of mentalizing in adults identified 57 instruments, and no two overlapped completely on the 18 components, 17 dimensions of mentalizing, and the relational context of the framework used to describe them (Hawksdale et al., 2025); likewise, tasks that share the construct name theory of mind measure different processes (Quesque & Rossetti, 2020). Different construct names also cover the same items: the same review included among measures of mentalizing, although with a differing focus, the Lack of Emotional Clarity and Awareness subscales of the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (Gratz & Roemer, 2004; Hawksdale et al., 2025, Table 10), so the same items are given the construct name of emotion regulation in one literature and of mentalizing in another. In participants' responses, theory of mind tasks correlate weakly with each other (Warnell & Redcay, 2019), and in a meta-analysis of the correlations among ten commonly measured emotion regulation strategies, none of the theory-based structural models fitted the data (Naragon-Gainey et al., 2017). Current reporting practices allow overlap of this kind to go undetected (Flake & Fried, 2020). Because the interdependence of the three capacities is posited at the level of construct names, and each construct is measured by a pool of items from a separate instrument and told apart mainly by the construct names of its subscales, an association between two such measures can have three sources: the words in which construct names and items are written, the instruments through which the constructs are observed, and the interdependence of the capacities themselves.

Semantic Embeddings and Construct Overlap

Semantic embeddings offer a way to compare construct names and items directly. Items, scales, and construct names are represented as vectors in a shared space, in which proximity reflects use in similar linguistic contexts, so that the similarity between two descriptions becomes measurable and reproducible (Hussain et al., 2024; Larsen & Bong, 2016; Rosenbusch et al., 2020). Wulff and Mata (2025) used such a space for several thousand personality items and the scales and construct names that organize them: semantic similarity predicted the empirical associations between items and between scales, and the space was used to flag candidate jingle and jangle fallacies and to propose a taxonomy with fewer constructs. The authors present these tools as an aid to expert deliberation (Wulff & Mata, 2025 , 2026) and caution that semantically similar constructs should not always be treated as identical (Wulff & Mata, 2026, p. 63). Part of this judgment rests on participants' responses: of the ten criteria proposed by Lawson and Robins (2021) to establish whether two constructs are siblings, closely related and still distinct, four are empirical and concern the observed nomological networks, the association between the measures, a common general factor, and incremental validity (see also Blötner, 2025).

Two questions remain open. First, does the agreement between items and participants' responses hold across questionnaires as well as within them? Wulff and Mata (2025) validated the semantic space against correlations collected in separate samples, one for each inventory, and used a sample that answered several inventories only to fine-tune the model. Items from the same questionnaire share authors, format, response scale, and often wording, so part of their correlation may come from the questionnaire itself. Separating this part requires the same participants to answer all the questionnaires, which is also the design required by the empirical criteria of Lawson and Robins (2021). Second, are the candidate fallacies flagged from the text confirmed by participants' responses? Wulff and Mata (2025) examined them by inspecting their items, without testing them against the responses of participants who completed both measures. These questions are especially pressing in a domain like clinical psychology. Wulff and Mata (2025) worked with broad personality inventories covering many distinct traits. Here, a few closely related constructs are measured with questionnaires that often share stems and response formats, so that items written for different constructs can be similar in wording, and part of their correlation may come from the questionnaires.

The Present Study

If a theoretical construct is the territory, its construct name, its items, and participants' responses are three maps of it. Building on this evidence, the present study asks whether these maps converge in measures of mentalizing, epistemic trust, and emotion regulation. In two large samples of emerging adults and adolescents who completed the Reflective Functioning Questionnaire for Youth (RFQY-13; Martin-Gagnon et al., 2023), the Epistemic Trust, Mistrust and Credulity Questionnaire (ETMCQ; Campbell et al., 2021), and the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale-Short Form (DERS-SF; Kaufman et al., 2016), we compared the construct names and items of their 11 subscales with participants' responses, with three specific aims.

First (Aim 1), we asked whether construct names identify their items, that is, whether the items of each subscale are semantically closer to its own construct name than to the construct names of the other subscales. Second (Aim 2), we asked whether the semantic similarity between items predicts the correlation between participants' responses to them, at the level of items and of subscales, and whether this holds both within and across questionnaires. Third (Aim 3), we asked whether participants' responses follow construct names or items: whether the correlations between subscales are more strongly associated with the similarity of their construct names or with the similarity of their items, over all pairs and for the candidate jingle and jangle fallacies flagged from text with an adaptation of the criterion of Wulff and Mata (2025).

We expected the semantic similarity between two items to be positively associated with the correlation between participants' responses to them (H1), and planned to describe the pairs at which the two disagree as candidate jingle-like and jangle-like pairs (H2). Because disruptions of social learning are hypothesized to underlie personality pathology, we also expected items to differ in their associations with the self and interpersonal domains of personality functioning (H3a), and items in jangle-like pairs to be more strongly associated with impairment than items without overlap (H3b). The item-level analyses were preregistered (https://osf.io/ka7d8).

Method

Transparency and Openness

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study. The study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework on January 12, 2026, before the data were accessed (https://osf.io/ka7d8). The registration covered the item-level analyses of the 46 items of the RFQY-13, the ETMCQ, and the DERS-SF in a sample of emerging adults. Everything else was added after the data had been accessed and is labeled as such; Table 1 lists every departure from the registration and every point it left open, with the reason. The analysis code, the item and label texts submitted to the embedding model, and the embeddings are available at https://osf.io/4s63z. The participant data are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

Participants and Procedure

Emerging Adults

Emerging adults aged 18 to 29 years and fluent in Italian were recruited through online snowball sampling on general social media platforms and were encouraged to share the invitation with peers from various social and occupational backgrounds to reach beyond university students. After giving informed consent online, they completed a 30-minute questionnaire on Qualtrics, with CAPTCHA verification at entry; participation was voluntary and uncompensated. Sample size was not set by a power analysis. The data had been collected within a larger survey and had not been accessed when the study was registered; the registration anticipated approximately 800 participants and the inclusion of all valid responses available at extraction. Of 1,470 participants with a completion time of at least 10 minutes, 1,167 (79.4%) had complete data on the three questionnaires and were retained as registered, so that every correlation is estimated on the same respondents. The excluded participants differed negligibly from the included ones on the RFQY-13 and ETMCQ subscales they had completed, except for a small difference on Certainty (d = -0.23). Mean age was 24.22 years (SD = 2.77). Sex assigned at birth was female for 72.1%; gender identity was female for 68.6%, male for 27.8%, and non-binary or another identity for 3.6%. Most described themselves as heterosexual (74.5%), 96.3% were born in Italy, 59.1% were students, and 65.1% held a university degree.

Adolescents

The adolescent sample was not part of the registration and was analyzed with the same code. Adolescents aged 14 years or older with adequate knowledge of Italian were recruited between April and June 2026 in secondary schools in northern Italy. Parents gave informed consent online, and adolescents gave their assent; the questionnaires were completed anonymously on Qualtrics during school hours, in the presence of the researchers and a teacher, and participation was voluntary and uncompensated.

Of 1,082 records, six were excluded for a completion time under 10 minutes or incomplete data, and eight because four participant codes appeared on two complete records each, which left 1,068 participants. Mean age was 16.71 years (SD = 1.28, range 14 to 20), across the five years of secondary school. Sex assigned at birth was female for 67.0%; gender identity was female for 65.6%, male for 32.8%, and non-binary, another identity, or not reported for 1.7%; 96.3% were born in Italy. The LPFS-BF was administered in some schools only and was completed by 661 participants, on whom the analyses involving the external criterion are based.

Both studies aligned with the Ethical Code of the American Psychological Association and with the Declaration of Helsinki, and the Ethics Committee of the University of Milano-Bicocca approved all materials and procedures.

Measures

The two samples completed the same Italian versions of the instruments.

Mentalizing.

The Reflective Functioning Questionnaire for Youth (RFQY-13; Martin-Gagnon et al., 2023) yields two subscales, Uncertainty about mental states (7 items) and Certainty about mental states (6 items), and was administered on a 7-point scale.

Epistemic trust. The Epistemic Trust, Mistrust, and Credulity Questionnaire (ETMCQ; Campbell et al., 2021; Liotti et al., 2023; Milesi et al., 2024) has 15 items rated on a 7-point scale and three subscales of five items: Trust, Mistrust, and Credulity. The Italian version has been validated in adults and adolescents.

Emotion regulation. The Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale-Short Form (DERS-SF; Kaufman et al., 2016; Mancinelli et al., 2024) has 18 items rated on a 5-point scale and six subscales of three items: Awareness, Clarity, Goals, Impulse, Nonacceptance, and Strategies.

The three Awareness items, the only reverse-keyed items in the set, were reversed.

Personality functioning. The Level of Personality Functioning Scale-Brief Form 2.0 (LPFS-BF; Hutsebaut et al., 2016; Weekers et al., 2019; Gritti et al., 2025) has 12 items rated on a 4-point scale and yields a Self and an Interpersonal domain.

Descriptive statistics, internal consistency, and the correlations among subscales are reported in Table 2. Every item correlated positively with the rest of its subscale in both samples. Note. Correlations of the emerging adults (EA, N = 1,167) below the diagonal and of the adolescents (Ado, N = 1,068) above it. Correlations with the LPFS-BF domains are computed on the participants who completed it (all emerging adults; 661 adolescents), and the two domains correlated .53 in the emerging adults and .64 in the adolescents. Means are item means on the original response scales (RFQY-13 and ETMCQ 1 to 7, DERS-SF 1 to 5, LPFS-BF 1 to 4), with Awareness items reversed so that higher scores indicate more difficulty. α = Cronbach's alpha.

Semantic Representations

We described each subscale in language in two ways, by its items and by its construct name. Both descriptions depend on text alone and are the same in the two samples.

Encoding. As registered, similarity was the cosine between multilingual sentence embeddings. After the text homogenization of Wulff and Mata (2025), which also removed a difference in final punctuation between instruments, the texts were encoded in Italian, the language of administration, with BGE-M3 (Chen et al., 2024) through sentence-transformers (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019). The model was chosen before any result was inspected because it is multilingual, open, runs locally, and has not been fine-tuned on psychometric items (Hussain et al., 2024; Wulff & Mata, 2026, p. 63); settings are given in Table S1.

Content space. Each item was represented by its vector and each subscale by the renormalized mean of its item vectors, as in Wulff and Mata (2025). Because cosines in such spaces are compressed (Ethayarajh, 2019), we interpret comparisons between matrices and statistics standardized within rows, and no absolute cosine.

Label space. Construct names were taken from the source publications (Campbell et al., 2021; Gratz & Roemer, 2004; Martin-Gagnon et al., 2023). The bare English name was designated as primary before any variant was inspected; because alignment is standardized within each row, encoding items in Italian and names in English affects all similarities of a row alike. Five other variants, in Italian, in a sentence frame, and as definitions, are reported in Table S4, and all texts submitted to the model in Table S2.

Statistical Analyses

All analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.0; R Core Team, 2026) with psych and qgraph, and in Python (Version 3.14.0) with sentence-transformers and PyTorch; package versions are given in Table S1, and the analysis code is available at https://osf.io/4s63z.

Responses and inference. As registered, item associations were estimated as polychoric correlations (cor_auto in qgraph); subscale associations were the Pearson correlations among subscale scores, as in Wulff and Mata (2025). Comparisons with semantic similarity use absolute correlations. Two similarity matrices were compared with the Pearson correlation over their pairs and tested with one-sided permutation (Mantel) tests. H1 is the confirmatory test; the other pvalues are uncorrected, and conclusions rest on effects that recur in both samples, which were analyzed separately with the same code and settings and were neither pooled nor compared statistically.

Aim 1. For each subscale, we computed the cosine between its items and each of the 11 construct names and report the z score and rank of its own construct name, as in Wulff and Mata (2025), tested against random reassignment of construct names to subscales.

Aim 2. We correlated the cosines between items with the absolute correlations between participants' responses over the 1,035 item pairs (H1) and, averaging both over the item pairs that join two subscales (Hussain et al., 2024), over the 55 subscale pairs. Because the same participants answered all items, pairs were also compared within subscales, within questionnaires, and across questionnaires, with the questionnaire as the method in the logic of the multitrait-multimethod matrix (Campbell & Fiske, 1959). As an illustration, Figure 1 places the items by classical multidimensional scaling of the two distances, 1 minus the cosine and 1 minus the absolute correlation.

Aim 3. Over the 55 subscale pairs, we tested whether the correlations between subscales were more strongly associated with the similarity of their items than with the similarity of their construct names, and report the partial correlation of each description controlling for the other.

Candidate fallacies were flagged with the criterion of Wulff and Mata (2025), adapted to 11 subscales: a jingle when construct names are similar and items distinct, and a jangle in the reverse case (flags under the original rule in Table S3). For each flagged pair we report whether participants' responses, ranked among the 55 pairs, side with the construct names or with the items, and give correlations corrected for attenuation.

Registered analyses H2 and H3.

Jingle-like item pairs have semantic similarity at or above the 80th percentile and response association at or below the 20th, and jangle-like pairs the reverse (H2). For H3a, each item was correlated with the Self and Interpersonal domains of the LPFS-BF. For H3b, items in jangle-like pairs were compared with items in no candidate pair on these correlations with two-sided Welch tests on Fisher-transformed values; the number of tails was not registered. Subscale scores were also correlated with the two domains, descriptively. Note. "As registered": the registered rule applied without change. "Specification": the registration was silent or underspecified, and the table states the choice made. "Departure": a choice that differs from the registration. "Addition": an analysis or sample not in the registration, decided after the data were accessed.

Results

Only H1 to H3 were preregistered; Aims 1 and 3, the comparisons by type of pair, and the subscale level of Aim 2 were added after the data had been accessed. Results that involve responses are reported for the emerging adults (N = 1,167) and the adolescents (N = 1,068) side by side. Results that depend on text alone (Aim 1 and the flags of Aim 3) are the same in the two samples. All conclusions held under the alternative null of reassignment within instrument, the five other variants of the construct names, and signed correlations (Supplementary Material, S4).

Does the Name of a Construct Identify the Items That Measure It?

The mean alignment between the content of a subscale and its own label was z = 0.69, against a maximum of 3.02. The own label was the closest for 4 of the 11 subscales, and its mean rank was 3.91. Both the mean alignment and the count at first rank exceeded chance (p < .001 and p = .001).

For all seven subscales whose own label did not come first, the closest label was Lack of emotional clarity: it stood nearer than their own label to the content of Uncertainty about mental states, of the three ETMCQ subscales, and of three DERS-SF subscales (Table 3). The subscales identified by their own label were Certainty about mental states, Lack of emotional clarity, Difficulties engaging in goal-directed behavior, and Impulse control difficulties. Three own labels were less similar to their items than the average label: Epistemic mistrust, Nonacceptance of emotional responses, and Limited access to emotion regulation strategies, which ranked last of 11. Alignment is the z score of the cosine between a subscale's content vector and its own label, against the 11 labels of that row. Rank is the position of a subscale's own label among the 11, ordered by similarity to that subscale's content. The nearest label is given where the rank is not first. Primary label space, bare English label. The values depend on text only and are the same in the two samples.

Does What the Items Say Match How People Answer?

The semantic similarity of two items predicted the strength of the association between their responses: over the 1,035 item pairs, r = .62 in the emerging adults and r = .58 in the adolescents (both p < .001; Table 4). H1 was supported, and the adolescent sample gave the same result. The correspondence was higher for pairs within a subscale (.71 and .59) and within an instrument across subscales (.67 and .60) than for pairs across instruments (.42 and .37), which were the majority of pairs (699 of 1,035; Figures S2 and S3); all tested values exceeded chance.

Figure 1 shows the two spaces side by side. In the semantic map the items group by instrument, with the DERS-SF, the RFQY-13, and the ETMCQ occupying separate regions; in the response map they group by whether they describe a difficulty or a capacity, with the items describing difficulties forming one region in which the three instruments are mixed, and Certainty, Trust, and Awareness forming three separate regions. Uncertainty and Clarity are adjacent in both maps. The adolescents gave the same picture (Supplementary Material, Figure S1). and of the response correlations (right), emerging adults

Points are items, marked by instrument; crosses and labels mark the centroid of each subscale. The first two dimensions account for 39% and 40% of the distances (rank correlation between the distances in the map and the input distances .71 and .87), so the figure illustrates the analyses in the text and supports no claim of its own.

Aggregated to the 55 subscale pairs, the correspondence was higher than at item level: r = .72 in the emerging adults (p < .001) and r = .66 in the adolescents (p = .002). It held within instruments (r = .75 and .69, p = .049 and .047), and across instruments it was lower and did not reach significance taken alone (r = .54 and .41, p = .057 and .196). The floor of the permutation test is 1 / 5,001; p < .001 is at the floor except for adolescent pairs within an instrument at item level (p = .0004).

Do the Responses Follow the Names or the Contents?

Over the 55 subscale pairs, the response correlations were related to the similarity of the contents (r = .46 and .41) and only weakly to the similarity of the names (r = .13 and .04). The difference between the two correlations, .34 and .38, was larger than under permutation of the response matrix (p = .006 and .002). Controlling for the contents, the names were negatively related to the responses (partial r = -.17 and -.25), and controlling for the names, the contents kept their association (partial r = .48 and .47).

The adapted criterion flagged six pairs in at least one of the 20 combinations of bounds (Table 5). The three jingles were all within an instrument, and their names share all words but one or differ by a prefix: Lack of emotional awareness with Lack of emotional clarity, Certainty with Uncertainty about mental states, and Epistemic credulity with Epistemic trust. The three jangles were Nonacceptance of emotional responses with Limited access to emotion regulation strategies, Epistemic mistrust with Uncertainty about mental states, the only pair across instruments, and Difficulties engaging in goal-directed behavior with Limited access to emotion regulation strategies.

For the five flagged pairs within an instrument, the rank of the response correlation was nearer to the rank of the contents than to that of the names in both samples. For the three jingles the responses ranked below the contents, further still from the names: Certainty and Uncertainty about mental states ranked 4th of 55 by name and correlated .06 and .13 (ranks 49 and 39). For the two DERS-SF jangles the responses ranked among the highest: Nonacceptance and Strategies was the most correlated pair in both samples (r = .67 and .79; corrected for attenuation, .79 and 1.10). For Epistemic mistrust with Uncertainty about mental states, 31st by name and 3rd by content, the response correlation of .45 ranked 17th in the emerging adults, at equal distance from the two descriptions, and that of .44 ranked 14th in the adolescents, nearer the contents; corrected for attenuation, .60 and .63. A pair is flagged when its names and its contents fall in opposite bands (jingle: names in the "same" band, contents in the "distinct" band; jangle: the reverse), with the bands given by the exact share of pairs within a construct for a lower bound of 2 to 5 and an upper bound of 6 to 10 constructs. Ranks are among the 55 subscale pairs, 1 for the most similar; response ranks use absolute correlations. Names and contents depend on text only and are the same in the two samples. In both samples the four items involved in jangle-like pairs were more strongly associated with both domains than the items that entered no candidate pair (34 in the emerging adults, 21 in the adolescents): .46 against .35 for Self, t(4.5) = 1.42, p = .223, and .36 against .28 for Interpersonal, t(5.7) = 2.15, p = .078, in the emerging adults; .43 against .31, t(8.0) = 2.20, p = .059, and .38 against .25, t(8.0) = 2.79, p = .024, in the adolescents. The difference had the registered direction in all four comparisons and reached significance in one. Two of the four items come from the subscales most strongly associated with the LPFS-BF (Uncertainty and Strategies), and the two Mistrust items include the one most associated with it, while the comparison group includes most Certainty items, so the difference partly reflects which subscales and items enter each group.

Registered Analyses

Exploratory Analysis: The Subscales and Personality Functioning

In both samples, Uncertainty about mental states and the DERS-SF subscales correlated more strongly with the Self than with the Interpersonal domain, except DERS-SF Awareness in the adolescents, while ETMCQ Mistrust and Credulity were associated with the two domains to the same degree (

Table 2, rows 12 and 13). ETMCQ Trust and RFQY-13 Certainty in the emerging adults, and DERS-SF Awareness in the adolescents, were unrelated to personality functioning (|r| < .10 with both domains); in the adolescents Trust and Certainty correlated .12 and .15 with the Self domain. The two RFQY-13 subscales thus differed sharply: Uncertainty correlated .65 and .57 with the Self domain, and Certainty -.02 and .15.

Discussion

In this contribution, we aimed to examine whether construct names, items, and participants' responses tell the same story about measures of mentalizing, epistemic trust, and emotion regulation, three capacities that theory describes as interdependent and that are measured with separate questionnaires. The three maps only partially converged, and in the same way in emerging adults and in adolescents: construct names rarely identified their own items, participants' responses followed the items, more closely within than across questionnaires, and where names and items disagreed about a pair of subscales, the responses sided with the items.

We take the three aims in turn, then ask what the pattern means for the three capacities, and finally what it means beyond them.

Construct Names Do Not Identify Their Items

Only four of the 11 construct names were the closest description of their own items, and the name that described most subscales best was Lack of emotional clarity. The second finding explains the first. Across the three questionnaires most items describe one experience, not knowing what one feels, thinks, or why one acts, and a name that states this experience fits them better than names such as Epistemic mistrust or Limited access to emotion regulation strategies, which state a theoretical construct and say little about the content of its items. This is a direct instance of the assumption on which jingle and jangle fallacies rest, that the name of a measure tells what it contains (Elson et al., 2023), and it departs from the close alignment between construct names and scale content found for personality inventories (Wulff & Mata, 2025, p. 947). Part of the gap lies in the names as input to a language model: they are short technical phrases, rare in general text, whose parts are related in ways a cosine does not express (Ciapparelli et al., 2025; Günther et al., 2019), and a phrase without context yields a less reliable representation than one drawn from its uses (Cassani et al., 2023). Placing the names in a sentence or replacing them with their definitions changed little, so in this domain the problem lies in the names, and the curation of construct labels that Wulff and Mata (2025, p. 951) call for would mean renaming subscales. For a reader of this literature, the practical point is simple: an argument built on construct names is built on the least reliable of the three maps.

Participants' Responses Follow the Items, Within the Instrument

The semantic similarity of two items predicted how strongly participants' responses to them were associated, as registered, which extends the validation of semantic embeddings in personality (Hussain et al., 2024; Wulff & Mata, 2025) to clinical constructs measured in Italian.

What the design adds is the comparison across questionnaires, which separate samples for each inventory could not provide, and here the correspondence was clearly lower. This is what the multitrait-multimethod logic anticipates when the questionnaire acts as a method (Campbell & Fiske, 1959): items written for the same instrument share authors, format, response scale, and often wording, and part of their agreement, in text as in responses, comes from the instrument.

Thus, in the semantic map the items are organized by instrument; in the response map they are organized by whether they describe a difficulty or a capacity, and the items describing difficulties from the three questionnaires occupy one region regardless of the instrument they come from. The text of the items is therefore a useful guide to how people will answer, and the two things it does not see are the method effect of the instrument and the axis along which the responses are actually organized. A second bound lies in what the two spaces represent: semantic models represent meaning at the level of a population of speakers (Günther et al., 2019), whereas a response records how one person read and endorsed a description (Schwarz, 1999), so the two can agree only as far as participants read the items alike.

The Candidate Fallacies Are Resolved by the Items

Where names and items disagreed about a pair of subscales, participants' responses followed the items in every pair within an instrument. The three jingles were pairs of subscales named on a common template, a choice often made precisely to tell subscales apart, and their responses were nearly independent. The two jangles within the DERS-SF were pairs whose names are distant and whose items share a stem, and their responses were among the most correlated of all, giving no support to the distinction the names suggest; by the empirical criteria of Lawson and Robins (2021), such pairs are candidates for siblings or for a single construct, a judgment that would also require evidence on their nomological networks and incremental validity. The one pair across instruments, Epistemic mistrust with Uncertainty about mental states, was the only case in which the responses stood between the two descriptions in the emerging adults, and nearer the items in the adolescents. The flags that a semantic screen produces are thus a starting point for judgment (Rosenbusch et al., 2020; Wulff & Mata, 2026), and in this item set every verdict but one went to the items.

What This Means for Mentalizing, Epistemic Trust, and Emotion Regulation

In the mentalizing approach, mentalizing, epistemic trust, and emotion regulation are linked within a social learning system, and their associations are read as evidence of this interdependence (Fonagy & Allison, 2014; Luyten et al., 2020). Three things in the present results bear on how such evidence should be read. 2), is a reading of the names; the items and the responses agree with the observation that the certainty-uncertainty dimension "may not be unidimensional" (Hawksdale et al., 2025, p. 15).

Second, the experience of not knowing what one feels sits at the center of the three instruments under three construct names. RFQY-13 Uncertainty and DERS-SF Clarity both describe it, one item of each is almost the same sentence, and their responses were closely related; the ETMCQ Mistrust item most associated with impaired personality functioning describes feeling that others do not understand what one wants or needs. The mentalizing approach places this experience under the self-oriented and affective poles of mentalizing (Fonagy & Luyten, 2009), research on emotion regulation calls it a lack of clarity (Gratz & Roemer, 2004), a review of mentalizing measures counts the DERS Clarity and Awareness subscales among them (Hawksdale et al., 2025), and in the theory the experience of having one's own mind understood is what opens epistemic trust (Fonagy & Allison, 2014). When the three questionnaires correlate, then, part of the correlation is this one experience described three times, and part is a general factor of difficulty that the response map makes visible, in which items from the three instruments form one region; whether that factor is the general vulnerability that disruptions of social learning are proposed to underlie (Fonagy et al., 2017; Luyten et al., 2020) or the direction in which the items are worded cannot be told apart in these data. The interdependence the theory proposes may well be real, but with these instruments it cannot be separated from shared wording and shared method, and what theory says about each construct applies only in part to what its items measure.

Third, the capacities stand apart. Epistemic trust, Certainty about mental states, and emotional awareness occupied their own regions of the response map, away from the difficulties, and were unrelated or weakly related to personality functioning in both samples, with the caveat that DERS-SF Awareness behaved differently in the adolescents (Mancinelli et al., 2024). In these instruments the social learning system is measured almost entirely from its deficit side, and the capacities that the theory describes as its working state are measured by subscales that do not covary with the rest.

For the researcher and the clinician in this field, the consequences are tangible. High scores on Uncertainty, Clarity, and Mistrust add less independent evidence than the names of three questionnaires suggest, and reading the items a patient endorsed turns the scores back into the clinical material they summarize. Studies that enter these subscales as separate predictors should expect their shared variance to be large and should avoid "mindlessly partialing out shared variance" (Lawson & Robins, 2021, p. 359). Validation studies of a new measure of any of the three capacities would gain from reporting its correlations with the instruments of the other two traditions, which are likely to be administered alongside it.

Beyond the Case Study

Mentalizing, epistemic trust, and emotion regulation are one case. What the case shows is a method and an order of reliability. Construct names, items, and participants' responses are three descriptions of the same constructs, and they can be compared in the same participants; when they are, the items are the description that the responses follow, the instrument sets the limit of that correspondence, and the names are the description to trust least. Wulff and Mata (2025) call the difficulty of comparing findings across construct taxonomies taxonomic incommensurability, a term Kuhn (1962) applied to scientific theories; here it arises in the words in which names and items are written and in the instruments through which the constructs are observed, and only what remains once both are accounted for can be attributed to the constructs themselves.

For research and reviews, the overlap between two measures is best checked through their items and participants' responses before they are combined, compared, or entered in the same model; coding studies by the content of their items (Hawksdale et al., 2025) and screening candidate groupings with semantic tools (Rosenbusch et al., 2020; Wulff & Mata, 2026) would make such decisions explicit, and such decisions are rarely reported (Flake & Fried, 2020). For instrument development, construct names could state what the items are about and which end of a specific dimension a high score indicates. Separating shared method from shared capacity, finally, requires observing the constructs with methods other than self-report, such as interviews scored for reflective functioning, behavioral tasks, and informant reports (Campbell & Fiske, 1959).

Limitations

We used a single embedding model, without a multiverse over alternative models (Steegen et al., 2016). Items were encoded in Italian and the primary construct names in English.

Many DERS-SF items share a stem, which can raise the similarity of items from the same instrument, and the subscale level rests on 55 pairs. Eight of the 11 subscales are worded as difficulties and three as capacities, so the direction of wording is confounded with construct in this item set. The samples differ in age, recruitment, and battery, and DERS-SF Awareness behaved differently in the adolescents, as in the Italian validation in adolescents (Mancinelli et al., 2024); differences between the samples cannot be attributed to age. All measures were single-occasion self-reports.

Conclusion

A theoretical construct is known through three descriptions: the name it is given, the items written to measure it, and the answers people give to those items. The present study compared the three in the same participants and found that they converged only in part.

Participants' responses followed the items, the instrument bounded that correspondence, and the names, the description on which theories are written and literatures are organized, were the least reliable of the three. In measures of mentalizing, epistemic trust, and emotion regulation, the interdependence that theory proposes among the three capacities could not be separated from the experience their items share and from the questionnaires through which they are observed.

The same comparison can be made wherever constructs theorized as related are measured with separate instruments, and until it is made, what theory says about a construct applies only in part to what its items measure.

H2.

The registered quintile rule yielded 8 jingle-like and 3 jangle-like item pairs in the emerging adults, and 20 jingle-like and 2 jangle-like pairs in the adolescents; six of the adolescent jingle-like pairs and both jangle-like pairs were also found in the emerging adults. Five of the six shared jingle-like pairs joined the RFQY-13 Certainty item stating that one usually knows exactly what other people are thinking with Trust and Credulity items of the ETMCQ, and the sixth joined a Trust and a Mistrust item. In the adolescents, 13 of the 20 jinglelike pairs involved the three reverse-keyed DERS-SF Awareness items. The jangle-like pairs found in both samples joined two Mistrust items of the ETMCQ with little shared vocabulary, a mismatch between wording and responses within one subscale, and an RFQY-13 Uncertainty item about not knowing why one acts as one does with the DERS-SF Strategies item about expecting to remain upset for a long time; in the emerging adults the first Mistrust item also formed a jangle-like pair with the same DERS-SF item. The four items involved in jangle-like pairs were the same in the two samples.

H3a.

As described by H3a, the subscales differed in their patterns of association with the two domains of the LPFS-BF, and the items of most subscales were more strongly associated with the Self than with the Interpersonal domain. The highest mean absolute correlations were those of DERS-SF Clarity (.58 with Self and .41 with Interpersonal), Strategies (.55 and .38), and RFQY-13 Uncertainty (.48 and .37) in the emerging adults, and of DERS-SF Clarity (.52 and .39), Goals (.52 and .41), and Strategies (.51 and .43) in the adolescents. The lowest were those of RFQY-13 Certainty (.03 and .06) and ETMCQ Trust (.05 and .07) in the emerging adults, and of DERS-SF Awareness (.01 and .03), ETMCQ Trust (.09 and .08), and RFQY-13 Certainty (.11 and .04) in the adolescents. ETMCQ Mistrust and Credulity were equally associated with the two domains. The Mistrust items differed among themselves, from the item about feeling that others do not understand what one wants or needs (.47 and .48 with Self) to the item about preferring to search the internet over asking other people (.22 and .15).

First,

Certainty and Uncertainty about mental states are two separate scales in these data, and only one of them measures personality impairment. Their names are among the most similar of the 55 pairs, their items describe different things, one's own feelings and other people's minds(Martin-Gagnon et al., 2023), their responses were nearly independent, and they differed sharply in their relation to personality functioning: Uncertainty was among the subscales most associated with the Self domain, Certainty showed no linear association with either domain, which leaves open the curvilinear relation that the hypermentalizing reading would predict for excessive certainty.
